items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?

options.text: We bought, rice eggs chillies and bananas.
options.why: The comma should separate the items, not come after bought.

options.text: We bought rice, eggs, chillies and bananas.
We bought rice eggs, chillies, and, bananas.
options.why: There should be a comma after rice, and no comma after and.

options.text: We bought rice, eggs, chillies, and, bananas.
options.why: There should be no comma after and.

hints: Find the items in the list.
Commas go between the items. The last two items are joined by and.
Say the list aloud and pause where each comma is. Does it sound right?
items.explanation: In a list, commas separate the items, and the last two are joined with and: rice, eggs, chillies and bananas.

items.prompt: Where should the comma go? After lunch we played football.

options.text: after lunch
after we
options.why: We is part of the main clause, so it should not be separated from played.

options.text: after played
options.why: Played and football belong together.

options.text: after football
options.why: The sentence ends after football, so it needs a full stop.

hints: The sentence starts with words that tell us when.
A comma usually follows a fronted adverbial, the phrase at the start that tells when, where or how.
Find the words that tell you when. Where do they end?
items.explanation: After lunch is a fronted adverbial telling us when, so a comma follows it: After lunch, we played football.

items.prompt: Which words could go in brackets? My cousin Raka who is ten plays the drums. Write them.
hints: Brackets hold extra information that the sentence could manage without.
Try reading the sentence and leaving out a group of words. Does it still make sense?
Read the sentence without three of its words. Which three can you take out?
items.explanation: Who is ten is extra information. The sentence still makes sense without it: My cousin Raka (who is ten) plays the drums.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses brackets correctly?

options.text: Borobudur (a huge temple) in Central Java) is visited by many people.
options.why: There is one opening bracket but two closing brackets.

options.text: Borobudur a huge temple (in Central Java is visited by many people.)
options.why: The brackets should go around the extra information only.

options.text: (Borobudur) a huge temple in Central Java is visited by many people.
options.why: Borobudur is the main subject, so it should not be in brackets.

options.text: Borobudur (a huge temple in Central Java) is visited by many people.

hints: Brackets come in pairs, around extra information.
Read each sentence without the words in brackets. It should still make sense.
Check that each sentence has one opening bracket and one closing bracket.
items.explanation: The extra information a huge temple in Central Java sits inside one pair of brackets, and the sentence makes sense without it.

items.prompt: Why are brackets used in this sentence? The Komodo dragon (the largest lizard in the world) lives on a few islands in Indonesia.

options.text: to show that someone is speaking
options.why: Speech marks show speech.

options.text: to separate the items in a list
options.why: Commas separate items in a list.

options.text: to add extra information that the sentence could manage without
to show the most important idea
options.why: The words in brackets are extra, not the main idea.

hints: Read the sentence without the words in brackets.
Does the sentence still make sense? Then think about what the brackets add.
Ask: is the information in brackets needed, or is it a bonus fact?
items.explanation: Brackets add extra information. The sentence makes sense without the words inside them.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences that use commas correctly to mark extra information.

options.text: Mr Tan, our new neighbour, grows chillies.
The mango which, was very ripe fell from the tree.
options.why: The commas should go before which and after ripe.

options.text: The mango, which was very ripe, fell from the tree.
Mr Tan our new, neighbour grows chillies.
options.why: The commas should go around our new neighbour.

options.text: My bag, is under the desk.
options.why: There is no extra information here, so no comma is needed.

hints: Extra information needs a comma before it and a comma after it.
Find the extra information in each sentence, then check where the commas are.
Read each sentence without the words between the commas. Does it still make sense?
items.explanation: In the correct sentences, the extra information our new neighbour and which was very ripe has a comma before it and a comma after it.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences: commas used correctly or needs fixing.

items.text: Although it was late, we kept reading.
The cat, sat on the mat.
Rudi, who loves maths, won a prize.
We had rice, fish, and, fruit.
If you are cold put on, a jumper.

hints: Look at where each comma is and why it is there.
Commas go after an opening clause or adverbial, around extra information and between list items.
Read each sentence aloud and pause at each comma. Does the pause make sense?
items.explanation: The correct sentences use a comma after an opening clause or adverbial and around extra information. The others put commas in places that split words that belong together.

items.prompt: A comma is missing. Write the word that the comma should come after. Although the road was flooded the bus kept going.
hints: The sentence starts with a subordinate clause.
When a subordinate clause comes first, a comma goes at the end of it.
Find where the although part ends and the main clause begins.
items.explanation: Although the road was flooded is a subordinate clause at the start, so a comma comes after flooded.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows clearly that the children washed themselves, and then the dog went for a walk?

options.text: After the children had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: Without a comma, it sounds as if the children washed the dog.

options.text: After, the children had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: A comma after After does not make sense here.

options.text: After the children had washed, the dog went for a walk.
After the children, had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: The comma splits the children from what they did.

hints: Read each sentence aloud, pausing at each comma.
A comma can show where one idea ends and the next begins.
Ask in each sentence: who or what did the washing?
items.explanation: The comma after washed shows that the first idea ends there. Without it, readers may think the children washed the dog.

items.prompt: How many commas does this sentence need? On Saturday morning Bu Rina who is our school nurse bought rice and chillies.
hints: Look for an opening phrase and for extra information.
An opening phrase needs one comma. Extra information needs a comma on each side.
Start with On Saturday morning. Where does it end?
items.explanation: The sentence needs three commas: On Saturday morning, Bu Rina, who is our school nurse, bought rice and chillies.

items.prompt: Maya packed a hat ___ a bottle and a towel.
hints: Maya packed three things.
In a list, we separate the items.
Look at what comes between "a hat" and "a bottle".
items.explanation: A comma separates items in a list. The last two items are joined by "and", so no comma is needed there.

items.prompt: Build the sentence. It has extra information about Tom between commas.
items.answer: Tom, my cousin, plays the drums.
hints: The extra information is about Tom.
Commas go before and after the extra information.
Start with the name, then the extra words.
items.explanation: "My cousin" is extra information about Tom, so it sits between two commas.

items.prompt: Which word should have a comma after it? When the bell rang the children ran outside.
hints: The sentence starts with a "when" part.
A comma separates the opening part from the main part.
Find where the opening part ends.
items.explanation: "When the bell rang" is the opening part. A comma goes after it, before "the children ran outside".

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by the job of the commas in them.

items.text: We need eggs, flour, sugar and butter.
Late in the afternoon, the rain stopped.
My teacher, Mr Hadi, plays the guitar.
Wulan packed pens, paper and a ruler.
After the match, we drank cold water.
The mango, still green, fell down.

hints: Look at where the commas sit in each sentence.
Pairs of commas around a phrase mark extra information.
Check the first words: do they set the scene before the main part?
items.explanation: Lists have commas between items, openers have one comma before the main part, and extra information sits between two commas.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly to add extra information?

options.text: The river, which was very wide flooded the village.
options.why: The second comma is missing after "wide".

options.text: The river which was very wide, flooded the village.
options.why: The first comma is missing after "river".

options.text: The river, which was very wide, flooded the village.
The, river which was very wide flooded the village.
options.why: The comma is in the wrong place.

hints: The extra information needs a comma at both ends.
Take the extra part out: does the sentence still work?
Check for one comma before "which" and one after "wide".
items.explanation: Extra information needs a comma before and after it. Without it the sentence still makes sense: "The river flooded the village."

items.prompt: Match each sentence to the job the punctuation does.
pairs: Bring pens, which are cheap, to school.
Before you start, read the rules.
hints: Look at which punctuation mark is used.
Only one sentence has brackets.
Count how many commas each sentence has and where they sit.
items.explanation: Brackets hold a small detail, list commas separate items, paired commas wrap extra information, and a single comma ends an opening phrase.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences where brackets are used correctly.

options.text: Our school (founded in 1980) has a big garden.
Our school (founded in 1980 has a big garden).
The kite (a red one) flew over the roof.
The kite a red one) flew over the roof.
(The kite) a red one flew over the roof.

hints: Brackets come in pairs.
The words inside should be extra information.
The sentence must still make sense without the bracketed part.
items.explanation: Correct brackets enclose only the extra detail, and the rest of the sentence still works without it.

items.prompt: Complete the table.
head: Sentence
Extra information
Punctuation used
hints: Look for the pair of marks around the extra part.
The extra information is the part you could remove.
Row 2 uses a different mark from commas.
items.explanation: The puppy sentence uses brackets, and in the last sentence the extra information is "who is tall".

items.prompt:
Read the play script. Which part should go in brackets?
Dewi: I do not want to go.
She looks at the floor.
Bayu: Please come with me.

options.text: Dewi: I do not want to go.
options.why: This is what Dewi says, so it is not a stage direction.

options.text: Bayu: Please come with me.
options.why: This is spoken dialogue.

options.text: She looks at the floor.
Please come
options.why: This is a spoken part and is not an action.

hints: In a script, some lines are spoken and some tell actors what to do.
Brackets hold stage directions.
Which line shows an action, not speech?
items.explanation: Stage directions tell the actor what to do. They are written in brackets, so (She looks at the floor.) is the answer.

items.prompt: Write the word that the missing comma should come after. Rangga, who had never swum before jumped into the pool.
hints: The first comma is already there.
Find where the extra information stops.
The extra part begins with "who".
items.explanation: The extra information "who had never swum before" needs a closing comma after "before".

items.prompt: Citra has more than one brother. Which sentence tells us that Bayu is the one we mean, without saying how many brothers she has?

options.text: Citra's brother Bayu is ten.
Citra's brother, Bayu, is ten.
options.why: With commas, Bayu is extra information, which suggests she has only one brother.

options.text: Citra's brother (Bayu) is ten.
options.why: Brackets also show extra information, so this suggests only one brother.

options.text: Citra's, brother Bayu, is ten.
options.why: The commas are in the wrong places.

hints: Think about whether "Bayu" is needed to know which brother.
Commas make a name extra information.
Without commas, the name tells us which brother.
items.explanation: Without commas, "Bayu" is needed to say which brother. With commas it would be extra, which suggests she has just one brother.

items.prompt: Kofi's favourite sport ___ football ___ is played all over the world.
hints: The word "football" is extra information.
Use brackets, a pair.
The first mark opens, the second closes.
items.explanation: Brackets open before "football" and close after it, because the sentence still works without the extra word.

items.prompt: Which version is punctuated correctly?

options.text: The festival, (which lasts a week), begins in June.
options.why: Brackets and commas together are not needed for the same extra information.

options.text: The festival (which lasts a week begins in June).
options.why: The bracket closes in the wrong place.

options.text: The festival which lasts a week, begins in June.
options.why: There is only one comma, so the extra information is not marked.

options.text: The festival (which lasts a week) begins in June.

hints: The extra information must be fully enclosed.
Do not use two kinds of punctuation for one detail.
Check where the closing bracket is.
items.explanation: The bracket pair encloses exactly "which lasts a week", and the main sentence works without it: "The festival begins in June."

items.prompt: How many commas does this sentence need? When the storm ended Tom's uncle who is a fisherman checked his nets boat and ropes.
hints: Look for an opening phrase, extra information and a list.
Extra information needs two commas.
Count: one after the opening, two around the extra part, then the list.
items.explanation: One after "ended", two around "who is a fisherman", and one in the list after "nets". That makes four.

items.prompt: True or false: Commas separate the items in a list, as in "I bought apples, pears and plums".

options.text: True
False

hints: Look at the list.
Items are separated.
Commas.
items.explanation: Commas separate list items. The last two items are usually joined with and.

items.prompt: True or false: Brackets are used to show where speech begins.

options.text: True
False

hints: What shows speech?
Brackets are for extra details.
Speech marks.
items.explanation: Speech marks show where speech begins. Brackets add extra information.

items.prompt: True or false: In the sentence "The dog (a brown spaniel) barked", the brackets add extra information.

options.text: True
False

hints: Remove the brackets part.
Does it make sense?
It is extra.
items.explanation: Brackets enclose extra information that is not essential to the sentence.

items.prompt: True or false: The sentence must stop making sense if you remove the words in brackets.

options.text: True
False

hints: Try removing them.
Are they essential?
The sentence still works.
items.explanation: Words in brackets are extra, so the sentence should still make sense without them.

items.prompt: True or false: The sentence "My brother, who is ten, plays football" uses a pair of commas to add extra information.

options.text: True
False

hints: What is extra?
Who is ten.
Commas on both sides.
items.explanation: A pair of commas can mark off extra information in the middle of a sentence.

items.prompt: True or false: When extra information is in the middle of a sentence, only one comma is needed at the start.

options.text: True
False

hints: Count the commas.
Both ends are needed.
A pair.
items.explanation: A pair of commas is needed, one before and one after, just like brackets.

items.prompt: Extra information can go inside ___.
hints: They look like curved lines.
They come in pairs.
They start with br.
items.explanation: Brackets can hold extra information in a sentence.
